questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain why (a) European powers were in a race to annex Cameroon and (b) Germany succeeded to annex the territory in 1884? In what ways did Cameroonians react to the German penetration and occupation by 1907?

(7/7/6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In the last quarter of the 19th century the coast of Cameroon, with its river estuaries, its harbours and its trading partners among the Duala, was wanted by Britain, France and Germany. Germany finally signed the decisive treaties in July 1884. The answer has three parts.

**(a) Why the European powers raced to annex Cameroon [7 marks].**
1. *Economic reasons.* The Industrial Revolution created a need for raw materials (palm oil, palm kernels, rubber, ivory, timber, cocoa lands) and for markets. The Duala were the main middlemen, so the coast was a profitable trading zone.
2. *Strategic reasons.* The coast of the Bight of Biafra, the Wouri estuary (Douala) and the foot of Mount Cameroon offered good harbours and a naval base on the route to the Gulf of Guinea, and a base to move into the interior.
3. *Rivalry between the powers.* After 1880 Britain, France and Germany competed for colonies for power and prestige. Fear that a rival might take the territory pushed each of them to hurry.
4. *Missionary and humanitarian influence.* British Baptist missionaries (Joseph Merrick, Alfred Saker) had been established at Douala and Bimbia and at Victoria, and the Basel Mission came in 1886; Britain was seen as the natural power on the coast. The anti-slave-trade treaties of 1840 had given Britain a special position.
5. *The Berlin Conference.* The Berlin West Africa Conference (1884-1885) established that a claim to African land had to be backed by effective occupation, which turned the rivalry into a race to sign treaties on the ground.
6. *The request of the Duala chiefs.* From about 1879 the kings of Bell and Akwa wrote letters to the British Government asking for a protectorate; the delay in replying left the way open to others.

**(b) Why Germany succeeded in 1884 [7 marks].**
1. *Pressure from German firms.* German trading houses on the coast (Woermann of Hamburg, and Jantzen and Thormaehlen) were already important and asked Bismarck for protection.
2. *A change in German policy.* Bismarck, who had at first been against colonies, changed his mind in 1884 for reasons of trade, national interest and domestic politics.
3. *A well-prepared mission.* The explorer Dr Gustav Nachtigal arrived on the warship *Moewe* in July 1884, with the authority to sign treaties.
4. *British delay.* The British Government was slow and hesitant: Consul Hewett arrived days after the Germans had signed the treaty and hoisted their flag. Britain was also concerned with the Niger area.
5. *The treaty with the Duala chiefs.* On 12 July 1884 the Duala kings Bell and Akwa signed the Germano-Duala Treaty with the representatives of the German firms. The German flag was raised in mid-July 1884 and the territory became a German protectorate (Kamerun). The chiefs gave up sovereignty, legislative power and administration, and they hoped to protect their middleman trade and obtain protection against their rivals.
6. *Rivalries among the Duala themselves* made it easier to obtain the signature of the main chiefs and to put down opposition afterwards.
7. *German naval and military strength* backed the claim; German gunboats supported the proclamation.

**(c) How Cameroonians reacted by 1907 [6 marks].**
1. *Armed resistance.* Several communities fought the German penetration: (i) the Bakweri of Mount Cameroon, under chief Kuva Likenye, fought the Germans in the early 1890s near Buea and other areas, and were defeated after a hard struggle; (ii) the Duala of Hickory Town and Joss Town resisted in 1884-1885 and were punished by German naval and military action; (iii) in the north the Fulani lamidates (such as Tibati, Ngaoundere and Garoua) were conquered around 1899-1901 after resistance; (iv) other peoples of the interior (Maka, Beti, Bulu and the Grassfields) resisted the German columns and the demand for labour at different times.
2. *Collaboration and alliance.* Some rulers cooperated to keep power or defeat rivals, for example King Njoya of Bamum and Chief Atangana of the Ewondo (Yaounde area). The Germans used them as intermediaries.
3. *Peaceful protest.* The Duala chiefs wrote petitions and complaints to the German authorities and later to the Reichstag against taxation, land seizure and ill-treatment, and they tried to keep their middleman trade.
4. *Flight and passive resistance.* Many people left their villages, hid in the forest, refused to carry loads or work for the Germans, or tried to evade tax and forced labour.
5. *Working for the new order.* Some Cameroonians accepted wage labour on the plantations and in the administration, or went to mission schools, to gain from the new situation.

**Conclusion.** The race for Cameroon was driven by trade, strategy and rivalry; Germany won in 1884 by treaty, preparation and British delay. By 1907 Cameroonians had reacted in many ways, but German superior arms generally prevailed.
